summary: PCEP has been extended to support stateful path computation, where the PCE tracks paths and resource use. Those extensions did not meet all the needs of GMPLS-controlled networks. This document adds the extensions to PCEP needed to use a stateful PCE in GMPLS networks.

eli5.summary: A route planner that remembers all current trips can plan better. This teaches it to do so for optical-style networks with special rules.

questions: what is the pcep lsp exclusion subobject
subtitle: How a stateful path computation server learns about, updates and creates optical-style GMPLS paths over PCEP.

tldr.problem: Stateful PCEP extensions did not cover everything GMPLS-controlled networks (such as optical and TDM networks) need, including switching types, labels, bidirectional paths and protection context.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9504 reuses the GMPLS objects from RFC 8779, adds three capability flags, a new LSP Exclusion subobject for route exclusion, a few LSP flags (G, B, RG), and new error codes.
tldr.outcome: A stateful PCE can report, update and initiate GMPLS LSPs over PCEP. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 9504 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted, so it remains the base specification for stateful PCEP in GMPLS networks, read together with that update.

sections.title: Why GMPLS Needs Its Own Stateful Extensions
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes traffic engineering paths. A stateless PCE keeps only the network topology and resource data in its TE Database. A stateful PCE also tracks the LSPs themselves. RFC 8231 lets a PCC delegate its LSPs to a stateful PCE, and RFC 8281 lets a PCE set up LSPs on its own initiative.

Both documents leave out technology-specific objects and do not cover GMPLS-controlled networks such as WSON, OTN and SONET/SDH. RFC 8779 extended PCEP for GMPLS, but only for stateless computation. RFC 9504 fills the gap and also covers PCE-initiated LSPs in GMPLS networks.
sections.eli5: There were already rules for a planner that remembers trips, and rules for planning in special networks. Nobody had said how to do both at once, so this document does.

sections.title: What GMPLS Adds as Requirements
sections.content:
Many requirements are shared with MPLS-TE and are already handled by RFC 8231 (update, delegation, state synchronization). RFC 9504 only addresses what is GMPLS specific:

  • Advertising the GMPLS stateful capability, in addition to the stateful PCE capability.
  • Carrying GMPLS switching capabilities (for example TDM, L2SC, OTN-TDM, LSC), the Generalized Payload Identifier (G-PID) and technology-specific traffic parameters (Tspec).
  • Label information. In a WDM network, path computation is tied to label selection, so a computed path is associated with a specific lambda and Explicit Label Control may be required.
  • Protection context, following RFC 4872 and RFC 4873.
sections.eli5: In a normal network, any road will do. In an optical network, a trip also needs a particular color of light all the way, so the planner must be able to say which color to use.

sections.title: Reusing Existing Messages and Objects
sections.content:
An active stateful PCE sends PCUpd messages to update delegated LSPs, and the PCC sends PCRpt messages to report changes. A passive stateful PCE uses PCReq and PCRep for computation and still receives PCRpt reports. A PCInitiate message asks an end node to set up an LSP. The GMPLS-specific attributes ride in these same messages.

Delegation, cleanup and remote LSP initiation from RFC 8281 apply to GMPLS LSPs without change. After a session starts, the PCE must learn the PCC's LSP state (LSP state synchronization) and stores it in the LSP-DB. Incremental synchronization is specified in RFC 8232.

Objects from RFC 8779 are used as they are: BANDWIDTH, LSPA, IRO, XRO and RP (with the Routing Granularity flag). The ERO is not extended. All stateful messages MUST include a Generalized END-POINTS object containing the LABEL-REQUEST TLV, and if unnumbered endpoints are used, the UNNUMBERED-ENDPOINT TLV MUST be used.
sections.eli5: The planner keeps using the same envelopes it always did. The new part is just extra notes inside, such as which kind of road and which color of light.

sections.title: Capability Flags and LSP Flags
sections.content:
The GMPLS-CAPABILITY TLV (value 45, from RFC 8779) in the OPEN object gets three new flags. Each must be advertised by both the PCC and the PCE before the matching message is allowed for GMPLS LSPs:

  • R (LSP-REPORT-CAPABILITY, bit 31): allows PCRpt.
  • U (LSP-UPDATE-CAPABILITY, bit 30): allows PCUpd.
  • I (LSP-INSTANTIATION-CAPABILITY, bit 29): allows PCE-initiated LSPs.

Three flags are also defined in the LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV of the LSP object (from RFC 9357), used in PCUpd, PCRpt and PCInitiate. G (bit 0) marks a GMPLS LSP. B (bit 1) is 0 for a unidirectional LSP and 1 for a bidirectional co-routed LSP. RG (bits 2-3) is the routing granularity: 01 node, 10 link, 11 label, with 00 reserved.
sections.eli5: Before the planner and the router work together on this, both have to raise their hands and say they know how. Then small tags on each trip say whether it is a special-network trip, whether it goes both ways, and how exact the route must be.

sections.title: The LSP Exclusion Subobject
sections.content:
RFC 5521 lets a PCC ask that certain nodes or links be excluded from a computed path. RFC 9504 adds a new subobject (type 11) to the XRO so a PCC can ask for a path that avoids everything used by another LSP, which is useful for building diverse paths.

The subobject has an X bit (0 means the exclusion MUST be honored, 1 means it SHOULD be), a type, a length, a reserved byte that MUST be zero on transmission, a flags byte (no flags are defined), and a Symbolic Path Name. The name has the same syntax as in RFC 8231: a string of printable ASCII characters, unique in the PCC. Because it is unique only at the head node, only LSPs sharing the same head node or PCC can be excluded.

The subobject MAY appear several times. When a stateful PCE receives it in a PCReq, it MUST look the LSP up in its LSP-DB and exclude every resource that LSP uses.
sections.eli5: It is like telling the planner: do not use any of the roads that trip number so-and-so uses, because I want a backup that does not share a road with it.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
All error handling in RFC 8779 still applies. RFC 9504 adds cases, mostly under Error-Type 19 ("Invalid Operation"):

  • Error-values 25, 26 and 27 cover a GMPLS update, report or instantiation attempted without the matching capability being advertised. The receiver SHOULD send a PCErr and end the session, though it MAY choose to use the capability anyway.
  • Value 23 means no LSP state is available for reoptimization. Value 24 means the LSP named in an LSP Exclusion subobject was not found; an implementation MAY instead ignore the exclusion.
  • Value 28 is used when the Generalized END-POINTS object appears for a non-GMPLS LSP, that is, the G flag is not set.

Under Error-Type 6 ("Mandatory Object missing"), the END-POINTS object missing for a GMPLS LSP, or a Generalized END-POINTS object without the LABEL-REQUEST TLV (Error-value 20), MUST be answered with a PCErr.
sections.eli5: If someone asks for something they never said they could do, or leaves out a required piece of the form, the other side sends back a note saying what went wrong.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5440, RFC 8231, RFC 8281 and RFC 8779 apply. The RFC says GMPLS extensions should be treated with the same security as for MPLS networks, and that the TLS-based secure transport of RFC 8253 can be used here too.

On the management side, the document makes no change to the basic operation of PCEP. It suggests that implementations allow configuring whether stateful GMPLS messages and constraints such as XRO are used. If detailed route information is included in state synchronization, the ingress node MUST carry the Record Route Object so that information can be collected.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is added to the lock on the door. The same protections as before still apply, and the old rules about who may talk to the planner still hold.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the three new bits in the "GMPLS-CAPABILITY TLV Flag Field" registry (29, 30 and 31), a new XRO subobject type (value 11, "LSP"), the G, B and RG bits in the "LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV Flag Field" registry, and the new error values.

IANA also created the "LSP Exclusion Subobject Flag Field" registry. Bits 0-7 are unassigned, and new values are assigned by Standards Action.
sections.eli5: The new numbers were written down in the official phone book so nobody else uses them for something different.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the subobject in bytes.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on transmission, ignored on receipt.

items.label: R
items.desc: LSP-REPORT-CAPABILITY: PCRpt allowed for GMPLS LSPs.

items.label: U
items.desc: LSP-UPDATE-CAPABILITY: PCUpd allowed for GMPLS LSPs.
